transcript:
This message comes from Schwab. At Schwab, you can get everything from self-directed investing to full-service wealth management, all in one place.
No matter your investing goal, life stage, amount to invest, or know-how, you can invest your way with Schwab.
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman, Brazil's defeated presidential candidate has arrived in the U.S.
NPR's Kerry Kahn reports the U.S. says it will provide visas to Flavio Bolsonaro and his family.
Live images show Flavio Bolsonaro and his family getting off a private airplane around 9.30 local time in Miami.
The family was escorted to an awaiting vehicle by uniformed officers carrying huge umbrellas obstructing views by gathered local media.
The dramatic arrival in the U.S. followed a whirlwind 36 hours since Bolsonaro refused to concede his loss to Brazilian President Luis Ignacio Lula da Silva.
As Supreme Court Justice ordered him to surrender his passport, Bolsonaro was facing multiple investigations, including money laundering charges.
He had defiantly pledged to lead the opposition against Lula. Yet overnight, Argentine officials said he crossed into the country, he then flew to Ecuador, and finally to the U.S.
Kerry Kahn, NPR News, Rio de Janeiro.
There is no indication Iran has tried to repair or reconstruct its nuclear facilities damaged by the U.S. and Israeli military strikes.
This is according to the head of the U.N. Nuclear Agency.
The agency also estimates Iran has a large stockpile of highly enriched uranium that is very close to the level needed for a nuclear weapon.
NPR's Hadil Al-Shalchi has more.
During a U.N. Security Council meeting on Tuesday, the International Atomic Energy Chief Rafael Grossi said the U.N. has been unable to verify the status of Iran's uranium stockpile and urged Iran to give inspectors access.
He said that despite the lack of on-the-ground monitors, there was still no evidence that Iran was trying to repair or reconstruct the nuclear sites damaged in recent U.S. Israeli strikes.
President Trump has said that one of his main reasons for going to war with Iran was to eliminate their capability to develop a nuclear weapon.
Last month, the agency's board referred Iran to the U.N. Security Council, saying the country was not cooperating with investigations to trace uranium.
Hadil Al-Shalchi, NPR News, Istanbul. Affordable housing is a key issue for many voters. NPR's Jennifer Ludden reports it is also motivating Gen Z candidates in statehouse races.
In Montana, 21-year-old Republican Lucas Schubert wants to create more starter homes young people can afford to buy.
That has been one of the biggest factors in development for the middle class in this country.
In New Haven, Connecticut, 26-year-old Democrat Eli Saban is a renter, unlike the vast majority of elected officials, and says that makes a difference.
I think it's the experience of being a renter and just the insecurity and instability that you feel.
Twenty-eight-year-old Democrat Olalea Anukulyade in Hartford appreciates the national conversation on housing.
But the action is happening at the state level.
Jennifer Ludden, NPR News.
You're listening to NPR.
Officials in Spain say that at least 68 people have died after a train collided with a second one today.
The second one was stopped on the tracks. Authorities fear the death toll will continue to rise.
Spanish government officials suggest human error is the cause of the accident, but no official cause has been disclosed.
In the U.S., the nation's organ donation system is making a big, controversial change to a rule that was designed to protect the safety of potential donors, and Piers Robstein has details.
The change is being made by the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network, which oversees the nation's organ system.
The move will relax what has been a strict firewall between the doctors caring for patients in the hospital and the organ procurement team standing by to try to retrieve their organs.
The change is part of a set of new policies designed to boost organ donations and minimize errors.
But critics worry it could put pressure on family members to discontinue care and deepen distrust in the organ system.
Robstein, NPR News.
The Federal Reserve concludes its two-day policy meeting today in Washington.
The Fed is widely expected to leave short-term interest rates alone.
The Milwaukee Brewers did not sweep at the World Series last night and defeated the Tampa Bay Rays, but the Brewers still lead the series three games to one.
Game five of the World Series is tonight at the Tampa Bay Rays home park in Florida.
You're listening to NPR.

topics.text: Brazil's defeated presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro arrives in Miami after refusing to concede
Iran shows no sign of rebuilding nuclear sites damaged by U.S. and Israeli strikes, says IAEA chief Grossi
Gen Z candidates Lucas Schubert, Eli Saban, and Olalea Anukulyade run for state office on housing affordability
At least 68 dead after a train collides with a stopped train in Spain
U.S. organ donation network relaxes firewall between hospital doctors and organ procurement teams
Federal Reserve concludes two-day policy meeting, expected to hold short-term interest rates steady
Milwaukee Brewers defeat Tampa Bay Rays in World Series Game 4, leading series three games to one
